USCIS may, in its discretion, use as advisory opinions statements submitted as expe1i testimony.
See Matter o.f Caron International, 19 I&N Dec. 791, 795 (Comm'r. 1988). However, USCIS is
ultimately responsible for making the final determination regarding a foreign national's eligibility
for the benefit sought. The submission of letters from experts supporting the petition is not
presumptive evidence of eligibility; USCIS may evaluate the content of those letters as to whether
they support the foreign national's eligibility. USCIS may give less weight to an opinion that is not
corroborated, in accord with other information or is in any way questionable. !d.; see also So_ffici,
22 I&N Dec. at 165 (citing Matter o.f Treasure Crafi: o.f Cal(fornia, 14 J&N Dec. at 190).
Furthermore, merely repeating the language of the statute or regulations does not satisfy the
petitioner's burden of proof. Fedin Bros. Co .. Ltd. v. Sava, 724 F. Supp. at 1108. The above
mentioned letters from do not establish that the Beneficiary's awards are nationally or
internationally recognized prizes or awards for excellence in the field.
In addition, the letters were not accompanied by other evidence that would sufficiently corroborate
the Petitioner's claim that the Beneficiary has won nationally or internationally recognized prizes for
excellence. Although the Petitioner submitted several foreign language articles that mention the
Beneficiary's results in competitions, the articles do not demonstrate that the awards the
received in competition are nationally or internationally recognized prizes or awards. Without
documentary evidence to provide information regarding the actual competitions themselves, such as
the level of those who participated, the selection criteria, or the degree of attention the events attract
within the field, we cannot conclude based on the name of the competitions alone that they are
national or international, and therefore that the results are recognized beyond the awarding entities as
national or international awards. A competition may be open to athletes from throughout a particular
country or countries, but this factor alone is not adequate to establish that an award or prize is
"nationally or internationally recognized." The burden is on the Petitioner to demonstrate the level
of recognition and achievement associated with the Beneficiary's awards.
Further, as noted by the Director, according to the awards certificates, the Beneficiary appears to
have participated only in age-restricted competition to date. The Petitioner also provided copies of
the Beneficiary's two 'in which his dancer proficiency classification and
competition results are recorded. While his proficiency level has progressed from ' as a young
child to the level of ' in 2012, the record does not demonstrate whether he achieved the highest
level of competition. Even within a national-level competition, an award given to an athlete
competing in age-restricted events at an intermediate level would not necessarily be "nationally
recognized."

Finally, the Petitioner has submitted documentary and testimonial evidence that several of the
Beneficiary's students have received awards in competition. However, since the Beneficiary did not
receive the awards, as required by the plain language of this criterion, we will examine this evidence
below in our discussion of the criterion at 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(B)(5).
In summary, the evidence is insufficient to establish that the Beneficiary received nationally or
internationally recognized prizes or awards for excellence.

Documentation of the alien's membership in associations in the .field for which
class(fication is sought, which require outstanding achievements of their members, as
judged by recognized national or international experts in their disciplines or fields.
8 C.F.R. § 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(B)(2).
In order to demonstrate that membership in an association meets this criterion, a petitioner must
show that the association requires outstanding achievement as an essential condition for admission to
membership. Membership requirements based only on employment or activity in a given field,
minimum education or experience, recommendations by colleagues or current members, or payment
of dues, do not satisfy this criterion, as such requirements do not constitute outstanding
achievements. Further, the overall prestige of a given association is not determinative; the issue is
membership requirements rather than the association's overall reputation.

The record does not establish that the Beneficiary has been employed in a critical or essential
capacity as a dance instructor for While the club's president conveyed her satisfaction with
his work as a dance instructor and overall job performance, the record does not sufficiently establish
that the Beneficiary's employment in the club was in a "critical or essential capacity." Rather, the
letters indicated that the Beneficiary is a talented instructor who performed his duties in a manner
that exceeded expectations during his employment.
In addition, the evidence does not demonstrate that has a distinguished reputation in the field.

Evidence that alien has either commanded a high salary or will command a high salary
or other remuneration for services, evidenced by contracts or other reliable evidence
8 C.F.R. § 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(B)(8).
The Petitioner has not provided evidence regarding the Beneficiary's past salary or remuneration. It has
instead stated that the Beneficiary meets this criterion based on his proffered annual salary of $37,000.
The Petitioner has provided wage data for three different occupational titles to establish that the
Beneficiary will earn a high salary: "dancer," "dancers and choreographers," and "coaches and scouts."
Of these, the occupation of "coaches and scouts" appears to be the most appropriate classification for
the Beneficiary's proffered position.
Regarding the Beneficiary's prospective salary, in response to the Director's RFE the Petitioner
provided comparative wage data from the Foreign Labor Certification (FLC) Data Center's Online
Wage Library (www.flcdatacenter.com) and from www.bls.gov relating to average or median wages
of "Coaches and Scouts" between May 2015 and June 2016, indicating a range of salaries between
$22,700 and $46,260 for New York area. The Petitioner also submitted
comparative wage data from www.bls.gov and from www.careeronestop.org relating to the national
salary range of "Coaches and Scouts" for May 2015, indicating a range of salaries for 2015 between
$19,930 and $70,050, and for 2014 between $17,570 and $68,950. Based on the submitted data for the
relevant occupation and time period, we do not conclude that the Beneficiary's proffered salary of
$37,000 qualifies as a high salary relative to similarly employed individuals. In light of the above, the
evidence submitted does not satisfy the plain language requirements of this criterion.
